payload.content: The chaining-degrades-more-gracefully claim implicitly assumes simple uniform hashing (each key equally likely to land in any bucket, independent of others) — stated explicitly after Craig questioned it. Under that assumption chain lengths cluster tightly around the load factor (Poisson-ish), so long chains are rare in practice — but chaining has no structural cap on chain length: a bad or adversarial hash function (hash-flooding attacks) can put all n keys in one bucket, giving O(n) worst-case lookup. Open addressing has a structural cap chaining lacks: since each slot holds exactly one key, no lookup can ever need more than m probes (table size) — worst case is bounded regardless of hash function quality. Net correction: 'open addressing degrades faster than chaining at the same load factor' is an average-case claim conditioned on a reasonable hash function, not a worst-case guarantee — worst-case the ranking flips, since chaining's downside is unbounded (can exceed table size m) and open addressing's is not.
payload.notes: Immediate follow-up to quiz_answered event 73 in the same session. This correctly identified an unstated assumption (uniform hashing) underlying the whole prior comparison. Walked through why the assumption usually holds in practice (Poisson-distributed chain lengths at a given load factor), then conceded the real point: chaining has no structural bound on chain length (vulnerable to bad hash functions / hash-flooding attacks, unbounded by table size m), while open addressing lookup is structurally capped at m probes regardless of hash quality — so the earlier ranking is an average-case-under-uniform-hashing statement, not a worst-case one, and worst-case the ranking actually reverses. Good example of Craig catching an implicit assumption rather than accepting the stated conclusion at face value.

payload.content: Dynamic array amortized doubling — why append is "amortized O(1)" despite occasional O(n) resize-copies. Fixed-increment growth (+k) produces resize copy-costs as an arithmetic sequence, summing to ~n^2/(2k) over n appends — average cost per append grows without bound as n grows (O(n), not O(1)). Doubling growth produces resize copy-costs as a geometric sequence, summing to ~2n over n appends — average cost per append settles at a constant regardless of n (true amortized O(1)). Worked both growth strategies by hand over 16 appends (step-by-step tables) to ground the asymptotic claim in concrete arithmetic, then projected to n=64 to show the fixed-increment average climbing while doubling stayed flat. Flagged open gap: general fact that a geometric series with any ratio > 1 sums to a bounded multiple of its largest term (needed to justify that x1.5 growth generalizes the same way) — not yet taught.

payload.content: Constant factors are dropped in Big-O -- O(log2 n) and O(log10 n) are the same class, differing only by a constant multiplier; convention uses base 2 because most log-time algorithms work by repeated halving. The halving mechanism: log_b(n) counts halvings, not items, so doubling n costs exactly one more step in log time versus n/2 more steps in linear time -- the actual mechanical reason logs are cheap. Best/worst/average case are a separate axis from growth-rate class; any of O(1)/O(log n)/O(n)/O(n^2) can carry any of the three. Unspecified Big-O defaults to worst case by convention, since it is the only guarantee that does not depend on assumptions about input distribution -- corrected from an initial average-case guess. Labeled best/worst/average breakdown of linear search (target at index 0 vs. index n-1/absent vs. uniformly distributed), worked as three short cases rather than one combined paragraph. payload.content: O(n log n) as uniform-cost: n operations each independently costing O(log n), worked via a balanced-tree build (n inserts, i-th insert costs ~log2(i)), table totaled by hand for n=8 and projected to n=64. The exact sum (log2(n!)) vs. the naive n*log2(n) estimate differs by a lower-order term, dropped by Big-O the same way constant factors are. Why the tree-build case is NOT amortized analysis: amortized analysis smooths a skewed sequence (rare expensive ops, many cheap ones); the tree build has no skew, every insert costs the same O(log n). Merge sort mechanics and why its O(n log n) is uniform across best/worst/average case: log n levels, O(n) merge work per level regardless of split. Merge sort use cases: guaranteed worst-case bound, stability, sequential access (linked lists, external sorting), O(n) extra space. Quicksort mechanics and its worst (O(n^2), imbalanced pivot) vs. average/best (O(n log n), balanced pivot) split. Quicksort use cases: in-place, cache locality, common stdlib default with pivot mitigation, not stable. Quicksort as the concrete example grounding the 2026-09-08 'unspecified Big-O defaults to worst case' convention. Corrected misconception: quicksort's O(n^2) worst case is best/worst/average-case variation within a single run, not amortized smoothing across a sequence of operations.

payload.content: Node structure (data + next pointer) and why nodes can be scattered anywhere in memory rather than adjacent. Pointer vs. reference distinction (address-holding, reassignable, no arithmetic vs. alias) -- clarified since Craig could describe the concept but not name the distinction. Traversal is O(n): no address-arithmetic shortcut exists for a linked list the way base+index*size works for arrays. Insert/delete broken into explicit cases: at head (O(1)), at tail (O(1) with a tail pointer, O(n) without), in the middle (O(1) splice once located, O(n) to locate). The singly-linked deletion gotcha: given a direct pointer to the node to delete, deletion is still O(n) because the predecessor (needed to relink around it) cannot be reached backward -- no back-pointer exists. Walked through with concrete addresses (0x1A00/0x3000/0x5000) after an initial misconception (assuming a pointer to the node also grants access to its predecessor). Connections: contrasts directly with Arrays (contiguous+O(1) index vs. scattered+O(1) splice-at-known-point); unlocks Trees (a tree node is a linked-list node with two 'next' pointers instead of one).

gaps.text: Two related misconceptions surfaced: (1) assuming a linked list's O(1) splice cost applies to 'reorder by content' operations that still require an O(n) search; (2) assuming a pointer to a node in a singly-linked list also grants access to the pointer that would need to change to delete it (its predecessor). Both stem from under-weighting the 'do I already have the pointer I need' precondition -- worth a light confirm-only check next review.

payload.notes: Follow-up scenario check immediately after Linked Lists teaching, same session. Two of three surfaced genuine misconceptions (both resolved with correction), one showed a strong independent extension beyond what was taught.

payload.content: prev/data/next node structure -- the direct fix for the singly-linked deletion gotcha, since the predecessor is now reachable from the node itself. Cost of the fix: pointer overhead roughly doubles per node (8 vs. 16 bytes on a typical 64-bit system), and every splice touches more pointers -- 4 for insertion (new node's prev+next, plus each neighbor's one link), 2 for middle-node deletion -- corrected mid-session after Craig cross-checked the general claim against the worked diagram and found insertion and deletion were being conflated. Deletion cases worked with diagrams: middle (2 pointer writes), head (skip the predecessor-side write -- no B.prev.next step exists), tail (mirror of head), single-node list (both neighbor-side writes are absent simultaneously -- needs an explicit guard, not just the two 'standard' branches). Misconception flagged: doubly-linked fixes navigation direction and O(1) deletion-by-pointer, not random access -- indexed lookup is still O(n). Deps: Linked Lists. Contrasts: Linked Lists (singly vs. doubly).
payload.notes: New section, split out of the Linked Lists teaching in the same session (not in the sidecar before today). Directly motivated by the singly-linked deletion gotcha from the Linked Lists session immediately prior. Craig's follow-up-quiz answer caught a real overgeneralization in the teaching material (see quiz_answered event same date) -- corrected on the spot.

questions.feedback: Correctly identified undo/redo as O(1) via prev/next respectively, and correctly explained a singly-linked list would fail this specific pattern since it has no way back to the previous state from a direct pointer to the current one.

Correctly derived the two-node head-deletion case (head=A.next, B.prev=null) unprompted, matching the head-deletion pattern taught earlier -- and caught a genuine imprecision in the teaching material: the earlier claim that 'every insert/delete touches four pointers' was true of insertion (new node's prev+next, plus each neighbor's link) but not of middle-node deletion, which the worked diagram itself showed as two writes. Corrected in follow-up.

Produced a mostly-sound framework (arrays for random access and near-end operations; singly-linked for cheap insertion near a known point; doubly-linked for cheap deletion near a known point) but omitted the precondition threaded through the whole session: all of those 'cheap' operations assume the node/position is already held, not searched for by content -- without it, insertion/deletion collapses back to O(n) regardless of list type. Also didn't name bidirectional-traversal-need (e.g. the undo/redo case just answered) as a driver independent of deletion speed.

gaps.text: The 'already holding the pointer vs. need to search for it' precondition -- the throughline of this whole session -- wasn't named as part of the general decision rule when asked to state one explicitly. Worth checking directly next review rather than assuming it transferred from the specific scenarios.

payload.notes: Follow-on quiz immediately after Doubly-Linked Lists teaching, same session as Linked Lists above. Two of three correct, including an instance of Craig catching an imprecision in the teaching material itself (see concepts_written on the taught event).

questions.feedback: Deletion of a middle node given only a direct pointer to it: correctly identified total cost as O(n), correctly explained that the predecessor address is unknown and must be found by a head-to-node traversal (O(n)), and correctly noted the splice itself is O(1) once the predecessor is in hand. Clean restatement of the 2026-09-11 gotcha with no prompting needed.

Deletion of the head node: correctly concluded O(1) and correctly reasoned that no predecessor lookup is needed since nothing precedes the head, and that the list already holds a direct reference to head (no traversal to find it) plus a single field read of head.next to find the new head. Used the word "cache" for why the head reference is instantly available -- flagged and corrected in session as imprecise (the O(1) access is because the list structure keeps head as a field, a structural fact, not because of CPU/memory caching, which is the separate cache-locality topic already flagged as a forward pointer). Did not affect the correctness of the complexity conclusion.

payload.notes:
Light confirm-only recheck of the two misconceptions from the 2026-09-11 Linked Lists session (reorder-by-content still needs O(n) search; a node pointer does not reach its predecessor), per that session's flagged gap. No new teaching -- two targeted scenario questions (middle-node deletion given a direct pointer vs. head deletion) probing exactly the precondition-awareness gap. Both answered correctly with sound reasoning; the underlying misconception from last time did not resurface.

Assessment notes: None substantive. One terminology note: used "cache" loosely for the head pointer being readily available; worth a one-line reminder next time cache locality (the actual hardware topic) comes up, so the two are not conflated.

questions.question: Say a team builds a "hybrid" mobile app -- not a full native app, just a thin wrapper that loads your website inside an embedded WebView (a browser window with no address bar). Would cookie-based session auth work the same way there as in a normal browser tab, or would it behave like a plain native app? Walk me through why.
questions.answer: Uncertain -- guessed cookies need to be stored in a browser's local cache and wasn't sure whether WebView has that option.
questions.feedback: Right instinct (it hinges on whether WebView has a cookie store) but no firm answer. Explained: a WebView is a full embedded browser engine (Chromium on Android, WebKit on iOS), so it carries the entire HTTP stack including the cookie jar -- cookie auto-attach works exactly like a normal tab. A plain native app has no such engine and makes raw network calls with no built-in cookie handling. This reframes the earlier 'closer to hardware' misconception (g62-1): it's not about hardware distance, it's about whether browser-engine code is present. Confirmed understood on follow-up.

questions.question: Say a site has a stored-XSS hole -- an attacker's script is running inside a logged-in user's page. The session cookie has HttpOnly and Secure set, but not SameSite. Can the attacker walk away with the cookie's actual value and reuse it later from their own machine? Can they still do damage while the script is running on the victim's page? Explain what's protected and what isn't, and why.
questions.answer: Correctly identified that the browser still auto-attaches the HttpOnly cookie to requests the injected script fires, so the attacker can act as the victim in the moment. Initially attributed a missing-SameSite scenario to the attacker being able to reuse the stolen cookie from their own machine later. Pushed back that this was really describing CSRF being possible without SameSite (a true statement) rather than theft-and-replay. Through discussion, correctly separated CSRF (blind -- the victim's own browser fires the forged request; the attacker never touches the cookie value) from theft-and-replay (governed entirely by HttpOnly, independent of SameSite), and concluded theft-and-replay specifically is not possible here because HttpOnly already blocks the script from reading the value.
questions.feedback: The hard part -- HttpOnly still lets the browser auto-attach the cookie to script-fired requests -- was right immediately. The gap: attributing cookie theft-and-replay to a missing SameSite flag. Corrected via the CSRF-is-blind framing (attacker never sees the value; it's the victim's own browser doing the work) vs. HttpOnly (the only thing governing whether the value can be read at all). Good-faith pushback with a real partial truth (missing SameSite does enable CSRF) led to a clean, fully self-derived final answer.

questions.question: You're choosing between session-based auth and JWTs for a new API behind a load balancer in front of 50 backend instances, and policy requires revoking a compromised credential within seconds. Which fits, and what's the actual cost of going the other way?
questions.answer: Session-based auth, because validity is a live server-side lookup that can be flipped immediately. JWTs have no such lookup -- a compromised token stays valid until its own expiry (e.g. 3600s) regardless of policy, and that window is the real cost of choosing JWTs here.
questions.feedback: Correct and complete -- named the underlying mechanism (server-side record vs. self-contained token) and the exact cost (the expiry window as an exploitable gap) with no prompting needed.

gaps.text: Retest of g62-1 ('why mobile favors tokens'), via a fresh WebView scenario rather than the original question: initial answer was uncertain rather than firmly wrong (correctly guessed it depends on whether WebView has a cookie store, but couldn't confirm). Explained that a WebView is an embedded browser engine (Chromium/WebKit) carrying the full HTTP stack including the cookie jar, vs. a plain native app which has no browser engine and makes raw calls with no built-in cookie handling. Confirmed understood on follow-up. Worth a light confirm-only check next review rather than a full re-teach.

Fresh gap, surfaced on an HttpOnly/XSS scenario: conflated a missing SameSite flag with enabling the XSS attacker to steal-and-replay the cookie from their own machine. Corrected by separating CSRF (a blind forged request the victim's own browser fires and attaches the cookie to -- the attacker never sees the value) from theft-and-replay (governed entirely by HttpOnly, independent of SameSite). Craig pushed back with the legitimate observation that missing SameSite does enable CSRF, and from there correctly re-derived that theft-and-replay specifically was not possible in this scenario given HttpOnly was set. Worth a light confirm-only check next review.
